name: Aisha Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build garden offices and timber cabins for a company that does about three a month, mostly for people working from home. I'm on the crew that goes out and builds them: base, frame, cladding, roof, windows, then the inside lining. A good one takes us six days from bare grass to keys. I like that the customer comes out every afternoon with tea and watches it grow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI come into your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to check the plans, work out materials, and in the evenings I use it to draw up designs for my own side jobs, small sheds and pergolas. My partner Wei is an electrician, and we've been talking about starting our own garden office firm together in a year or two. My parents run a restaurant, so I grew up watching people run their own business, and we've got about three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are still useful, and anyone who isn't using them is missing out. At work I'd keep showing the crew how I price things. Online I'd post a few of my designs, because that's good advertising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means our plan for the business still works. If AI stays a tool, it gives a small firm like ours a head start on design and quotes. That's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the company, keep doing two or three weekend jobs a month, and save toward starting the firm. Wei and I would aim to launch in about eighteen months. I'd start a simple website and a page for our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents feel about you starting a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud, and worried about the hours. My dad worked seven days for twenty years and he'd tell me not to do that. But he'd be the first to lend us his van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before launching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of savings, a couple of regular customers, and insurance. I'd also want one apprentice by year two, because that's how I learned and somebody should do the same for the next one.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are still useful and anyone not using them is missing out. I'd show the crew how I price things and post my designs online as advertising.
S0.think: Our business plan still works, because AI as a tool gives a small firm a head start on design and quotes.
S0.do: Keeps working at the company and doing two or three weekend jobs a month while saving to launch a firm with her partner in about eighteen months. Sets up a simple website and a page for their work.
S0.feel: Calm and impatient to get going.
S0.quote: My dad worked seven days for twenty years and he'd tell me not to do that.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is entrepreneurial, shaped by her parents' restaurant. She already uses AI daily and sees it as an advantage for small firms. She wants to train an apprentice, which fits her views on work and skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people willing to work and learn. I wouldn't moan about it, I'd say get on with it. Businesses that adapt will grow, that's how it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's perfect timing for us. If more people work from home because of AI, they want garden offices. And if AI cuts the cost of design and admin, a two-person firm can compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the launch forward to within a year. I'd use AI for designs, quotes and bookings from day one, and buy a cutting machine that works from the design files once we had steady work. I'd look at any robot tools for lifting panels, because my back won't last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Properly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good design program and the cutting machine, maybe four or five thousand together. We'd put in some savings and borrow the rest from my parents, not a bank. They'd want it paid back, though, my mum keeps a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you think would lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms that don't change, like my current boss, who still does quotes on paper. I like him, but if he won't change, customers will go elsewhere. That's not cruel, that's business.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity for people willing to work and learn, and businesses that adapt will grow, like always.
S1.think: It's perfect timing, because more home workers want garden offices and AI cuts design and admin costs for a two-person firm.
S1.do: Brings the business launch forward to within a year, using AI for designs, quotes and bookings from day one. Spends four or five thousand on design software and a cutting machine, borrowing from her parents rather than a bank, and looks at robot lifting tools.
S1.quote: They'd want it paid back, though, my mum keeps a notebook.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as pure opportunity and would move her plans forward. Her money comes from family, not banks, which fits her views. She's blunt that firms that won't adapt will lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people should look for the opportunities rather than wait for the government. I'd say that online and probably get shouted at. I'd still believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be less sure than I sound. If robots can build a garden office, the big firms will do it cheaper than us. Our chance would be getting in early and being the local name people trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch straight away, not wait, and rent robot tools as soon as they're available rather than buy. I'd keep Wei's wage coming in for safety while I run the firm. I'd lean on my parents for space and advice, and keep the costs tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and nervous at the same time, like before a big pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're less sure than you sound. What's the worry underneath?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my customers lose their jobs too. If everybody working from home is replaced, nobody needs a garden office. Then it doesn't matter how good my robots are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go back to my parents' restaurant for a while, I suppose. Or find whatever people still need built. There's always something, even if it's not what I planned.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be hard, but people should look for opportunities rather than wait for the government. I'd say it online and get shouted at.
S2.think: I'd be less sure than I sound, because big firms with robots would undercut us. Our chance would be getting in early and being the trusted local name.
S2.do: Launches the business straight away, renting robot tools rather than buying, while her partner keeps his wage for safety. Leans on her parents for space and advice and keeps costs tiny.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and nervous at once.
S2.quote: If everybody working from home is replaced, nobody needs a garden office.
S2.fieldNote: Her public line stays bold and pro-market, while privately she sees the risk to her customers. She'd act fast, keeping costs low and her partner's wage as a safety net. Her family's restaurant is her fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to get ahead. I'd tell people to start learning and stop complaining. I'd post a lot about what we were doing, because that brings in work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build the firm and pay off my parents. We'd be one of the first local firms using robots, and that could carry us. After that, I don't know, but I'd have something to sell or adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch within six months, and buy one robot tool once the first ones prove reliable, probably year two. I'd take on an apprentice in year one, so they learn the new way of building. And I'd save a slice of every job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice when robots are coming. Isn't that unfair to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because I'd teach them to run the robots as well as use a saw. Somebody has to know how a building goes together. I'd rather they learn that with me than nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Wei think of the timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd want to wait a bit longer, he's more careful. We'd argue and then meet in the middle, probably six months. That's how we usually work.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a chance to get ahead and tell people to start learning and stop complaining. I'd post a lot about our work because it brings in jobs.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build the firm and repay my parents, and being one of the first local firms with robots could carry us.
S3.do: Launches within six months, buys one robot tool once they prove reliable around year two and takes on an apprentice in year one. Saves a slice of every job.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, like a race she can win.
S3.quote: I'd teach them to run the robots as well as use a saw.
S3.fieldNote: Five years feels like the right amount of runway for her plan. She'd still train an apprentice, just in both old and new methods. Her partner is the cautious voice, and they meet in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and learn the machines. That's what I'd be saying everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is great for us. We'd have time to grow the firm, maybe take on two or three people, and bring robots in when they're ready. I'd be 37 with a proper business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch within the year as planned, and learn everything I can about the robot kit as it comes out. I'd buy robots in stages, never on big loans. I'd keep an apprentice on every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get comfortable and stop watching. My dad says the restaurants that close are the ones that stopped changing the menu. I'd keep changing the menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm with our name on the van, a few people we trained ourselves, and customers who come back. Maybe the robots do the heavy work and we do the design and the care. That's a good life.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work, and tell young people to learn a trade and learn the machines.
S4.think: Ten years is great for us, with time to grow the firm, take on a few people and bring robots in when ready. I'd be 37 with a proper business.
S4.do: Launches within the year, learns the robot kit as it comes out and buys robots in stages without big loans. Keeps an apprentice on every year.
S4.quote: My dad says the restaurants that close are the ones that stopped changing the menu.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year version fits her ambitions completely. Her main worry is getting complacent, and she borrows her father's restaurant lessons to guard against it. She imagines robots doing the heavy work while people do design and care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my customers would be hit at the same time as my trade, and that's a double hit. What would help is keeping taxes and red tape low for small firms so we can grow and hire. And keeping apprenticeships going, so young people have a way in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family. My parents' restaurant is my safety net, and it's why I'm not scared to take a risk. Not everyone has that, and I know I'm lucky.

headlineQuote: My parents' restaurant is my safety net, and it's why I'm not scared to take a risk.
portrait: Aisha Zhang is a 27-year-old carpenter who builds garden offices and cabins, uses AI every day and plans to start her own firm with her partner Wei, an electrician. They have about three months saved, and her parents' restaurant is her safety net and source of loans. She's calm when AI fizzles or changes things steadily, and sees steady change as perfect timing for her business. AGI in two years makes her uneasy, mostly because her customers might lose their jobs too, but she'd still launch at once on rented robots. With five or ten years she's confident she can build a firm, buy robots in stages and train apprentices.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her customers would be hit at the same time as her trade.
whatWouldHelp: Low taxes and little red tape for small firms so they can grow and hire, and keeping apprenticeships going.
